devanagari: देहिनोऽस्मिन्यथा देहे कौमारं यौवनं जरा । / तथा देहान्तरप्राप्तिर्धीरस्तत्र न मुह्यति ॥2.13॥
iast: dehino'sminyathā dehe kaumāraṃ yauvanaṃ jarā । / tathā dehāntaraprāptirdhīrastatra na muhyati ॥2.13॥
sayIt: day-hi-NO-smin ya-THAA DAY-hay kow-MAA-ram YOW-va-nam ja-RAA / ta-THAA day-HAAN-ta-ra-PRAAP-tir DHEE-ras TA-tra na MUH-ya-ti
translation: Just as the embodied self passes through childhood, youth, and old age in this body, so at death it passes into another body; the wise person is not confused by this.
source: Bhagavad Gita 2.13, Sanskrit Wikisource contributors, CC BY-SA, https://sa.wikisource.org/wiki/%E0%A4%AD%E0%A4%97%E0%A4%B5%E0%A4%A6%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%97%E0%A5%80%E0%A4%A4%E0%A4%BE/%E0%A4%B8%E0%A4%BE%E0%A4%99%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%96%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%AF%E0%A4%AF%E0%A5%8B%E0%A4%97%E0%A4%83; translation: Dharma Daily draft, pending review

words.meaning: is not deluded, is not confused

meaning: This is Krishna's first argument to Arjuna: the self that inhabits the body is not the body. Within one lifetime you already survive constant change — the child's body is gone, the youth's body is going — yet "you" persist through all of it. Death, the verse says, is one more such passage. For a daily practice, this is training in not panicking at change. Traditions read the "embodied one" differently — Advaita sees one Self appearing in many bodies, while Vishishtadvaita and Dvaita see many real individual souls — but all agree that the steady person is not thrown by the body's changes.
reflection: The body changes constantly — what in you has watched all of it change?

translations.hi: जैसे देहधारी आत्मा इसी देह में बचपन, यौवन और बुढ़ापे से गुज़रती है, वैसे ही मृत्यु पर वह दूसरी देह में प्रवेश करती है; धीर व्यक्ति इससे विचलित नहीं होता।

meanings.hi: यह अर्जुन के लिए कृष्ण का पहला तर्क है: देह में रहने वाला आत्म देह नहीं है। एक ही जीवन के भीतर आप निरंतर परिवर्तन से गुज़रकर बचते आए हैं — बच्चे की देह जा चुकी, युवा की जा रही है — फिर भी "आप" इन सबके बीच बने हुए हैं। श्लोक कहता है, मृत्यु ऐसा ही एक और पड़ाव है। दैनिक साधना के लिए यह परिवर्तन पर न घबराने का प्रशिक्षण है। "देही" कौन है, इसे परंपराएँ अलग-अलग पढ़ती हैं — अद्वैत अनेक देहों में झलकता एक ही आत्म देखता है, जबकि विशिष्टाद्वैत और द्वैत अनेक वास्तविक, अलग-अलग जीवात्माएँ — पर सब सहमत हैं कि धीर व्यक्ति देह के परिवर्तनों से विचलित नहीं होता।

devanagari: मात्रास्पर्शास्तु कौन्तेय शीतोष्णसुखदुःखदाः । / आगमापायिनोऽनित्यास्तांस्तितिक्षस्व भारत ॥2.14॥
iast: mātrāsparśāstu kaunteya śītoṣṇasukhaduḥkhadāḥ । / āgamāpāyino'nityāstāṃstitikṣasva bhārata ॥2.14॥
sayIt: maa-traa-spar-SHAAS too kown-TAY-ya shee-TOSH-na-soo-kha-DUH-kha-daah / aa-ga-maa-PAA-yi-no NIT-yaas taans ti-TIK-shas-va BHAA-ra-ta
translation: Contacts between the senses and their objects, Arjuna, bring cold and heat, pleasure and pain. They come and go and do not last — endure them patiently, Bharata.
source: Bhagavad Gita 2.14, Sanskrit Wikisource contributors, CC BY-SA, https://sa.wikisource.org/wiki/%E0%A4%AD%E0%A4%97%E0%A4%B5%E0%A4%A6%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%97%E0%A5%80%E0%A4%A4%E0%A4%BE/%E0%A4%B8%E0%A4%BE%E0%A4%99%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%96%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%AF%E0%A4%AF%E0%A5%8B%E0%A4%97%E0%A4%83; translation: Dharma Daily draft, pending review

words.meaning: contacts of the senses with their objects

meaning: Heat and cold, pleasure and pain arrive through the senses, stay a while, and leave. The verse does not tell you to stop feeling; it tells you to notice that sensations are visitors, not residents, and to practise titikṣā — patient endurance — while they pass. For daily practice this is immediately usable: the discomfort of sitting still, an irritating commute, a late-night craving are all "contacts of the senses," impermanent by nature. Commentators across traditions treat this verse in essentially the same way, as basic training in steadiness — the entry-level discipline on which the Gita's later teachings build.
reflection: What discomfort today can you meet as weather — passing, and bearable?

translations.hi: हे कौन्तेय, इंद्रियों का विषयों से स्पर्श ही सर्दी-गर्मी और सुख-दुख देता है। वे आते-जाते हैं, टिकते नहीं — हे भारत, उन्हें धैर्य से सहन कर।

meanings.hi: गर्मी-सर्दी, सुख-दुख इंद्रियों के रास्ते आते हैं, कुछ देर ठहरते हैं और चले जाते हैं। श्लोक यह नहीं कहता कि महसूस करना बंद करो; वह कहता है कि ध्यान दो — संवेदनाएँ मेहमान हैं, स्थायी निवासी नहीं — और उनके गुज़रने तक "तितिक्षा", यानी धैर्यपूर्ण सहनशीलता, का अभ्यास करो। दैनिक अभ्यास के लिए यह तुरंत काम आता है: स्थिर बैठने की असुविधा, खीझ दिलाने वाला सफ़र, देर रात की तलब — ये सब "इंद्रियों के स्पर्श" हैं, स्वभाव से ही अनित्य। टीकाकार परंपराओं के आर-पार इस श्लोक को लगभग एक ही तरह लेते हैं — स्थिरता का बुनियादी प्रशिक्षण, वह शुरुआती अनुशासन जिस पर गीता की आगे की शिक्षाएँ खड़ी होती हैं।

devanagari: न जायते म्रियते वा कदाचिन्नायं भूत्वा भविता वा न भूयः । / अजो नित्यः शाश्वतोऽयं पुराणो न हन्यते हन्यमाने शरीरे ॥2.20॥
iast: na jāyate mriyate vā kadācinnāyaṃ bhūtvā bhavitā vā na bhūyaḥ । / ajo nityaḥ śāśvato'yaṃ purāṇo na hanyate hanyamāne śarīre ॥2.20॥
sayIt: na JAA-ya-tay MRI-ya-tay vaa ka-DAA-chin NAA-yam BHOOT-vaa bha-vi-TAA vaa na BHOO-yah / a-JO NIT-yah SHAASH-va-TO-yam poo-RAA-no na HAN-ya-tay han-ya-MAA-nay sha-REE-ray
translation: The self is never born and never dies; having existed, it never ceases to be. Unborn, eternal, everlasting, and ancient, it is not slain when the body is slain.
source: Bhagavad Gita 2.20, Sanskrit Wikisource contributors, CC BY-SA, https://sa.wikisource.org/wiki/%E0%A4%AD%E0%A4%97%E0%A4%B5%E0%A4%A6%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%97%E0%A5%80%E0%A4%A4%E0%A4%BE/%E0%A4%B8%E0%A4%BE%E0%A4%99%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%96%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%AF%E0%A4%AF%E0%A5%8B%E0%A4%97%E0%A4%83; translation: Dharma Daily draft, pending review

words.meaning: nor will it again cease to be

meaning: This is the Gita's most famous statement about the self: it was never born, so it can never die. Bodies begin and end; the one who wears them does not. The verse piles up four words — unborn, eternal, everlasting, ancient — to hammer home that death touches only the instrument. Traditions differ on what this deathless self is: Advaita reads it as the one universal Self, while Vishishtadvaita and Dvaita read it as each individual soul, eternally real and distinct. Either way, for daily practice the verse invites a gradual loosening of the habit of thinking "I am only this body."
reflection: If the deepest part of you cannot be harmed, what would you attempt?

translations.hi: आत्मा न कभी जन्म लेती है, न मरती है; एक बार होकर वह फिर कभी होना बंद नहीं करती। अजन्मी, नित्य, शाश्वत और पुरातन यह आत्मा शरीर के मारे जाने पर नहीं मरती।

meanings.hi: आत्म के बारे में यह गीता का सबसे प्रसिद्ध कथन है: वह कभी जन्मा ही नहीं, इसलिए मर भी नहीं सकता। देहें शुरू और ख़त्म होती हैं; उन्हें पहनने वाला नहीं। श्लोक चार शब्द एक साथ रखता है — अजन्मा, नित्य, शाश्वत, पुरातन — यह पक्का करने के लिए कि मृत्यु केवल उपकरण को छूती है। यह अमर आत्म आख़िर क्या है, इस पर परंपराएँ भिन्न हैं: अद्वैत इसे एक ही सर्वव्यापी आत्मा के रूप में पढ़ता है, जबकि विशिष्टाद्वैत और द्वैत हर जीवात्मा को नित्य रूप से वास्तविक और भिन्न मानते हैं। दोनों ही स्थितियों में, दैनिक साधना के लिए यह श्लोक "मैं बस यह शरीर हूँ" की आदत को धीरे-धीरे ढीला करने का न्योता है।

devanagari: कर्मण्येवाधिकारस्ते मा फलेषु कदाचन । / मा कर्मफलहेतुर्भूर्मा ते सङ्गोऽस्त्वकर्मणि ॥2.47॥
iast: karmaṇyevādhikāraste mā phaleṣu kadācana । / mā karmaphalaheturbhūrmā te saṅgo'stvakarmaṇi ॥2.47॥
sayIt: kar-mun-YAY-vah-dhi-KAA-ras-tay maa pha-LAY-shoo ka-DAA-cha-na / maa kar-ma-pha-la-HAY-toor-bhoor maa tay SUN-go-stva-KAR-ma-ni
translation: Your right is to the action alone, never to its results. Do not make the results of action your motive, and do not become attached to inaction.
source: Bhagavad Gita 2.47, Sanskrit Wikisource contributors, CC BY-SA, https://sa.wikisource.org/wiki/%E0%A4%AD%E0%A4%97%E0%A4%B5%E0%A4%A6%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%97%E0%A5%80%E0%A4%A4%E0%A4%BE/%E0%A4%B8%E0%A4%BE%E0%A4%99%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%96%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%AF%E0%A4%AF%E0%A5%8B%E0%A4%97%E0%A4%83; translation: Dharma Daily draft, pending review

words.meaning: do not become one whose motive is the result of action

meaning: Probably the most quoted verse of the Gita. You are entitled to the effort, never to the outcome — so act fully, and stop negotiating with results. The verse closes both escape routes: do not work only for the reward, and do not use detachment as an excuse to quit acting. For daily practice it is a working instruction: show up, do the task well, release the scoreboard. Commentators genuinely diverge on its depth — Advaita reads desireless action as purifying the mind on the way to knowledge, while Vishishtadvaita and Dvaita read it as acting in service of and surrender to the Lord — and the verse itself supports both readings.
reflection: What task today deserves your full effort — with the outcome released?

translations.hi: तेरा अधिकार केवल कर्म पर है, उसके फलों पर कभी नहीं। कर्म के फल को अपना मक़सद मत बना, और अकर्म से भी तेरा लगाव न हो।

meanings.hi: शायद गीता का सबसे अधिक उद्धृत श्लोक। तुम्हारा हक़ प्रयास पर है, परिणाम पर कभी नहीं — इसलिए पूरे मन से कर्म करो, और नतीजों से सौदेबाज़ी बंद करो। श्लोक बचने के दोनों रास्ते बंद कर देता है: सिर्फ़ इनाम के लिए काम मत करो, और वैराग्य को काम छोड़ने का बहाना भी मत बनाओ। दैनिक अभ्यास के लिए यह एक काम करने लायक निर्देश है: हाज़िर रहो, काम अच्छे से करो, स्कोरबोर्ड छोड़ दो। इसकी गहराई पर टीकाकार सचमुच बँटे हुए हैं — अद्वैत निष्काम कर्म को ज्ञान की राह पर मन को शुद्ध करने वाला पढ़ता है, जबकि विशिष्टाद्वैत और द्वैत इसे भगवान की सेवा और शरणागति में किया गया कर्म — और श्लोक स्वयं दोनों पाठों को जगह देता है।

devanagari: योगस्थः कुरु कर्माणि सङ्गं त्यक्त्वा धनंजय । / सिद्ध्यसिद्ध्योः समो भूत्वा समत्वं योग उच्यते ॥2.48॥
iast: yogasthaḥ kuru karmāṇi saṅgaṃ tyaktvā dhanaṃjaya । / siddhyasiddhyoḥ samo bhūtvā samatvaṃ yoga ucyate ॥2.48॥
sayIt: yo-GAS-thah KOO-roo kar-MAA-ni SUN-gam TYAKT-vaa dha-nan-JA-ya / sid-dhya-SID-dhyoh sa-MO BHOOT-vaa sa-MAT-vam YO-ga OOCH-ya-tay
translation: Established in yoga, do your work, Arjuna, letting go of attachment, staying even in success and failure. That evenness of mind is called yoga.
source: Bhagavad Gita 2.48, Sanskrit Wikisource contributors, CC BY-SA, https://sa.wikisource.org/wiki/%E0%A4%AD%E0%A4%97%E0%A4%B5%E0%A4%A6%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%97%E0%A5%80%E0%A4%A4%E0%A4%BE/%E0%A4%B8%E0%A4%BE%E0%A4%99%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%96%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%AF%E0%A4%AF%E0%A5%8B%E0%A4%97%E0%A4%83; translation: Dharma Daily draft, pending review
meaning: This verse gives the Gita's working definition of yoga: samatvaṁ yoga ucyate — evenness is yoga. Not postures, not withdrawal from the world, but doing your work while staying level through success and failure. "Established in yoga" comes first; the acting flows from that steadiness rather than producing it. For a daily practice this reframes the goal: the win is not the result of the task but the evenness you kept while doing it. Commentators across traditions agree on the core instruction — abandon attachment, stay equal — though they differ, as with 2.47, on whether that equanimity ultimately serves knowledge or devotion.
reflection: What would evenness look like in your hardest hour today?

translations.hi: हे धनंजय, योग में स्थित होकर, आसक्ति त्यागकर, सिद्धि और असिद्धि में सम रहते हुए अपने कर्म कर। यही समता योग कहलाती है।

meanings.hi: यह श्लोक योग की गीता वाली कार्यकारी परिभाषा देता है: "समत्वं योग उच्यते" — समता ही योग है। न आसन, न संसार से पलायन, बल्कि सफलता और असफलता के बीच स्तर बनाए रखते हुए अपना काम करना। "योग में स्थित" पहले आता है; कर्म उस स्थिरता से बहता है, उसे पैदा नहीं करता। दैनिक अभ्यास के लिए यह लक्ष्य को नए सिरे से गढ़ता है: जीत काम का नतीजा नहीं, वह समता है जो आपने काम करते हुए बनाए रखी। मूल निर्देश पर — आसक्ति छोड़ो, सम रहो — सभी परंपराओं के टीकाकार सहमत हैं, हालाँकि 2.47 की तरह यहाँ भी वे इस पर भिन्न हैं कि यह समता अंततः ज्ञान की सेवा करती है या भक्ति की।

devanagari: ध्यायतो विषयान्पुंसः सङ्गस्तेषूपजायते । / सङ्गात्संजायते कामः कामात्क्रोधोऽभिजायते ॥2.62॥
iast: dhyāyato viṣayānpuṃsaḥ saṅgasteṣūpajāyate । / saṅgātsaṃjāyate kāmaḥ kāmātkrodho'bhijāyate ॥2.62॥
sayIt: DHYAA-ya-to vi-sha-YAAN POOM-sah SUN-gas tay-SHOO-pa-JAA-ya-tay / sun-GAAT san-JAA-ya-tay KAA-mah kaa-MAAT KRO-dho-bhi-JAA-ya-tay
translation: When a person keeps dwelling on the objects of the senses, attachment to them arises; from attachment desire is born, and from desire anger arises.
source: Bhagavad Gita 2.62, Sanskrit Wikisource contributors, CC BY-SA, https://sa.wikisource.org/wiki/%E0%A4%AD%E0%A4%97%E0%A4%B5%E0%A4%A6%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%97%E0%A5%80%E0%A4%A4%E0%A4%BE/%E0%A4%B8%E0%A4%BE%E0%A4%99%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%96%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%AF%E0%A4%AF%E0%A5%8B%E0%A4%97%E0%A4%83; translation: Dharma Daily draft, pending review

words.meaning: for one who keeps dwelling on

meaning: This is the Gita's precise psychology of how self-control fails. It never starts with the dramatic act; it starts with dhyāyataḥ — dwelling on, replaying, browsing. Attention lingers on an object, lingering becomes attachment, attachment sharpens into desire, and desire blocked becomes anger. The verse matters for practice because it locates the point of intervention early: you cannot easily fight a full-grown craving, but you can notice where attention is parked. Watching what the mind rehearses in idle moments is the daily discipline this verse suggests. Commentators across traditions read this chain in essentially the same way.
reflection: What do you keep returning to in thought — and where is it leading you?

translations.hi: विषयों का चिंतन करते रहने वाले व्यक्ति में उनके प्रति आसक्ति पैदा होती है; आसक्ति से कामना जन्म लेती है, और कामना से क्रोध उपजता है।

meanings.hi: आत्म-संयम कैसे टूटता है, इसका यह गीता का सटीक मनोविज्ञान है। शुरुआत कभी किसी नाटकीय कृत्य से नहीं होती; वह "ध्यायतः" से होती है — सोचते रहने, दोहराने, टटोलते रहने से। ध्यान किसी विषय पर ठहरता है, ठहरना आसक्ति बनता है, आसक्ति कामना में पैनी होती है, और रोकी गई कामना क्रोध बन जाती है। अभ्यास के लिए श्लोक इसलिए महत्वपूर्ण है कि वह हस्तक्षेप का बिंदु बहुत पहले पकड़ लेता है: पूरी बढ़ चुकी तलब से लड़ना आसान नहीं, पर यह देखना संभव है कि ध्यान कहाँ खड़ा किया हुआ है। खाली क्षणों में मन क्या दोहरा रहा है, इस पर नज़र रखना ही वह दैनिक अनुशासन है जो यह श्लोक सुझाता है। इस शृंखला को टीकाकार परंपराओं के आर-पार लगभग एक ही तरह पढ़ते हैं।

devanagari: क्रोधाद्भवति संमोहः संमोहात्स्मृतिविभ्रमः । / स्मृतिभ्रंशाद्बुद्धिनाशो बुद्धिनाशात्प्रणश्यति ॥2.63॥
iast: krodhādbhavati saṃmohaḥ saṃmohātsmṛtivibhramaḥ । / smṛtibhraṃśādbuddhināśo buddhināśātpraṇaśyati ॥2.63॥
sayIt: kro-DHAAD BHA-va-ti sam-MO-hah sam-mo-HAAT smri-ti-vi-BHRA-mah / smri-ti-bhran-SHAAD bood-dhi-NAA-sho bood-dhi-naa-SHAAT pra-NASH-ya-ti
translation: From anger comes delusion; from delusion, confusion of memory; from confusion of memory, the loss of discernment; and when discernment is lost, a person is ruined.
source: Bhagavad Gita 2.63, Sanskrit Wikisource contributors, CC BY-SA, https://sa.wikisource.org/wiki/%E0%A4%AD%E0%A4%97%E0%A4%B5%E0%A4%A6%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%97%E0%A5%80%E0%A4%A4%E0%A4%BE/%E0%A4%B8%E0%A4%BE%E0%A4%99%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%96%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%AF%E0%A4%AF%E0%A5%8B%E0%A4%97%E0%A4%83; translation: Dharma Daily draft, pending review
meaning: This completes the chain begun in 2.62: anger clouds judgment, clouded judgment scrambles memory — you forget what you know, what you value, who you are — and with memory gone, discernment (buddhi) collapses. When discernment goes, the person "perishes": commentators broadly agree this means not physical death but the ruin of falling from one's own path. For daily practice, the chain works as a diagnostic tool: when you catch yourself acting against your own values, trace backwards — the failure usually began much earlier, in what the mind was quietly dwelling on. The practice is interrupting the chain at its earliest visible link.
reflection: When anger last clouded you, what did you stop seeing?

translations.hi: क्रोध से मोह पैदा होता है; मोह से स्मृति का भ्रम; स्मृति के भ्रम से बुद्धि का नाश; और बुद्धि के नाश से मनुष्य नष्ट हो जाता है।

meanings.hi: यह 2.62 में शुरू हुई शृंखला को पूरा करता है: क्रोध निर्णय को धुंधला करता है, धुंधला निर्णय स्मृति को उलझा देता है — आप भूल जाते हैं कि क्या जानते हैं, आपके मूल्य क्या हैं, आप कौन हैं — और स्मृति के जाते ही विवेक (बुद्धि) ढह जाता है। विवेक के जाने पर व्यक्ति "नष्ट" होता है: टीकाकार मोटे तौर पर सहमत हैं कि इसका अर्थ शारीरिक मृत्यु नहीं, अपने ही मार्ग से गिर जाने की बर्बादी है। दैनिक अभ्यास के लिए यह शृंखला निदान का औज़ार है: जब आप खुद को अपने मूल्यों के विरुद्ध जाते पकड़ें, तो पीछे की ओर खोजिए — चूक प्रायः बहुत पहले शुरू हुई थी, उसमें जिस पर मन चुपचाप टिका हुआ था। साधना है — शृंखला को उसकी सबसे पहली दिखने वाली कड़ी पर तोड़ देना।

devanagari: या निशा सर्वभूतानां तस्यां जागर्ति संयमी । / यस्यां जाग्रति भूतानि सा निशा पश्यतो मुनेः ॥2.69॥
iast: yā niśā sarvabhūtānāṃ tasyāṃ jāgarti saṃyamī । / yasyāṃ jāgrati bhūtāni sā niśā paśyato muneḥ ॥2.69॥
sayIt: yaa ni-SHAA sar-va-bhoo-TAA-naam TAS-yaam JAA-gar-ti san-ya-MEE / YAS-yaam JAA-gra-ti bhoo-TAA-ni saa ni-SHAA PASH-ya-to moo-NAYH
translation: What is night for all beings is when the self-controlled one is awake; and what beings are awake in, the seeing sage knows as night.
source: Bhagavad Gita 2.69, Sanskrit Wikisource contributors, CC BY-SA, https://sa.wikisource.org/wiki/%E0%A4%AD%E0%A4%97%E0%A4%B5%E0%A4%A6%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%97%E0%A5%80%E0%A4%A4%E0%A4%BE/%E0%A4%B8%E0%A4%BE%E0%A4%99%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%96%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%AF%E0%A4%AF%E0%A5%8B%E0%A4%97%E0%A4%83; translation: Dharma Daily draft, pending review
meaning: A deliberately paradoxical verse: the sage is awake in what is night for everyone else, and asleep to what everyone else is awake in. What most people never notice — the inner self, the steady witness — is where the disciplined person is most alert; what most people chase — acquisition, status, sensation — the sage treats as darkness. It is a description, not a boast: as practice deepens, values quietly invert. For a daily practitioner the verse works as a check-in question: which of the two "days" am I currently awake in? Commentators across traditions read the image in essentially this way.
reflection: What matters to you that the world around you barely notices?

translations.hi: जो सब प्राणियों के लिए रात है, उसमें संयमी जागता है; और जिसमें प्राणी जागते हैं, देखने वाले मुनि के लिए वही रात है।

meanings.hi: जान-बूझकर विरोधाभासी श्लोक: मुनि उसमें जागता है जो बाकी सबके लिए रात है, और उसके प्रति सोया रहता है जिसमें बाकी सब जागते हैं। जिस पर अधिकांश लोग कभी ध्यान नहीं देते — भीतर का आत्म, स्थिर साक्षी — वहीं अनुशासित व्यक्ति सबसे सजग रहता है; और जिसके पीछे अधिकांश लोग दौड़ते हैं — संग्रह, हैसियत, संवेदना — उसे मुनि अँधेरा मानता है। यह डींग नहीं, वर्णन है: साधना गहराने के साथ मूल्य चुपचाप उलट जाते हैं। दैनिक साधक के लिए यह श्लोक एक जाँच-प्रश्न की तरह काम करता है: इन दो "दिनों" में से मैं अभी किसमें जागा हुआ हूँ? टीकाकार परंपराओं के आर-पार इस छवि को लगभग इसी तरह पढ़ते हैं।

devanagari: आपूर्यमाणमचलप्रतिष्ठं समुद्रमापः प्रविशन्ति यद्वत् । / तद्वत्कामा यं प्रविशन्ति सर्वे स शान्तिमाप्नोति न कामकामी ॥2.70॥
iast: āpūryamāṇamacalapratiṣṭhaṃ samudramāpaḥ praviśanti yadvat । / tadvatkāmā yaṃ praviśanti sarve sa śāntimāpnoti na kāmakāmī ॥2.70॥
sayIt: aa-poor-ya-MAA-nam a-cha-la-pra-TISH-tham sa-moo-DRAM AA-pah pra-vi-SHAN-ti YAD-vat / TAD-vat KAA-maa yam pra-vi-SHAN-ti SAR-vay sa SHAAN-tim aap-NO-ti na kaa-ma-KAA-mee
translation: As waters flow into the ocean, which stays full and unmoved as they enter, so all desires enter the one who attains peace — not the one who runs after desires.
source: Bhagavad Gita 2.70, Sanskrit Wikisource contributors, CC BY-SA, https://sa.wikisource.org/wiki/%E0%A4%AD%E0%A4%97%E0%A4%B5%E0%A4%A6%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%97%E0%A5%80%E0%A4%A4%E0%A4%BE/%E0%A4%B8%E0%A4%BE%E0%A4%99%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%96%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%AF%E0%A4%AF%E0%A5%8B%E0%A4%97%E0%A4%83; translation: Dharma Daily draft, pending review

words.meaning: the desirer of desires, one who chases desires

meaning: The ocean image: rivers pour in constantly, yet the ocean stays full and does not overflow or change its level. Likewise, desires and impressions keep arriving in the mind of a settled person — the verse does not promise they stop — but they enter without displacing that person's fullness. Peace, on this teaching, comes not from arranging the world so that nothing provokes desire, but from an inner fullness that arriving desires cannot destabilise. The contrast is the kāma-kāmī, the desirer of desires, who chases each river upstream. For daily practice: aim at fullness, not at a world with no rivers.
reflection: What desire could you let arrive — and pass — without chasing it today?

translations.hi: जैसे जल की धाराएँ समुद्र में मिलती जाती हैं और वह भरता हुआ भी अचल बना रहता है, वैसे ही जिसमें सारी कामनाएँ समा जाती हैं वही शांति पाता है — कामनाओं के पीछे भागने वाला नहीं।

meanings.hi: समुद्र की छवि: नदियाँ निरंतर उसमें उँड़ेलती रहती हैं, फिर भी समुद्र भरा रहता है — न उफनता है, न अपना स्तर बदलता है। वैसे ही एक ठहरे हुए व्यक्ति के मन में कामनाएँ और छापें आती रहती हैं — श्लोक यह वादा नहीं करता कि वे रुक जाएँगी — पर वे आकर भी उसकी पूर्णता को हिला नहीं पातीं। इस शिक्षा में शांति संसार को इस तरह सजाने से नहीं आती कि कुछ भी कामना न जगाए, बल्कि उस भीतरी पूर्णता से आती है जिसे आती हुई कामनाएँ डिगा नहीं सकतीं। इसके उलट है "कामकामी" — कामनाओं का कामी — जो हर नदी के पीछे उलटी धारा में दौड़ता है। दैनिक अभ्यास के लिए: निशाना पूर्णता पर रखिए, ऐसे संसार पर नहीं जिसमें कोई नदी ही न हो।

devanagari: विहाय कामान्यः सर्वान् पुमांश्चरति निःस्पृहः । / निर्ममो निरहंकारः स शान्तिमधिगच्छति ॥2.71॥
iast: vihāya kāmānyaḥ sarvān pumāṃścarati niḥspṛhaḥ । / nirmamo nirahaṃkāraḥ sa śāntimadhigacchati ॥2.71॥
sayIt: vi-HAA-ya kaa-MAAN yah sar-VAAN poo-MAANSH cha-ra-ti nih-SPRI-hah / nir-ma-MO ni-ra-hun-KAA-rah sa SHAAN-tim a-dhi-GACH-cha-ti
translation: The person who abandons all desires and moves through life free of craving, without any sense of "mine" or "I", attains peace.
source: Bhagavad Gita 2.71, Sanskrit Wikisource contributors, CC BY-SA, https://sa.wikisource.org/wiki/%E0%A4%AD%E0%A4%97%E0%A4%B5%E0%A4%A6%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%97%E0%A5%80%E0%A4%A4%E0%A4%BE/%E0%A4%B8%E0%A4%BE%E0%A4%99%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%96%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%AF%E0%A4%AF%E0%A5%8B%E0%A4%97%E0%A4%83; translation: Dharma Daily draft, pending review

words.meaning: having given up, having set down

meaning: The closing movement of chapter 2's portrait of the settled person. Peace comes to the one who moves through life having set down craving, possessiveness ("mine"), and self-importance ("I"). The verse names three distinct releases — desires, ownership, ego — suggesting they are separate habits to work on, not one switch. For daily practice it is concrete: notice each time "mine" or "I did that" tightens the chest, and loosen it once. Traditions differ on the endpoint — Advaita reads the dissolution of ego-sense as realising the one Self, while devotional schools read it as humility and surrender before the Lord — but the practice of loosening is shared.
reflection: What one claim of "mine" feels heaviest right now?

translations.hi: जो व्यक्ति सारी कामनाएँ त्यागकर, लालसा से मुक्त होकर, "मेरा" और "मैं" के भाव के बिना जीवन में चलता है, वही शांति पाता है।

meanings.hi: अध्याय 2 में ठहरे हुए व्यक्ति के चित्र की यह समापन-गति है। शांति उसे मिलती है जो लालसा, ममता ("मेरा") और अहंभाव ("मैं") को उतारकर जीवन में चलता है। श्लोक तीन अलग-अलग त्याग गिनाता है — कामनाएँ, स्वामित्व, अहं — जो संकेत है कि ये अलग-अलग आदतें हैं जिन पर काम करना है, कोई एक स्विच नहीं। दैनिक अभ्यास के लिए यह ठोस है: हर बार जब "मेरा" या "यह मैंने किया" छाती को कसता महसूस हो, उसे एक बार ढीला कीजिए। अंतिम मुक़ाम पर परंपराएँ भिन्न हैं — अद्वैत अहंभाव के विलय को एक ही आत्म की अनुभूति के रूप में पढ़ता है, जबकि भक्ति-परंपराएँ इसे भगवान के सामने विनम्रता और शरणागति — पर ढीला करने की साधना साझा है।

devanagari: न कर्मणामनारम्भान्नैष्कर्म्यं पुरुषोऽश्नुते । / न च संन्यसनादेव सिद्धिं समधिगच्छति ॥3.4॥
iast: na karmaṇāmanārambhānnaiṣkarmyaṃ puruṣo'śnute । / na ca saṃnyasanādeva siddhiṃ samadhigacchati ॥3.4॥
sayIt: na kar-ma-NAAM a-naa-RUM-bhaan naish-KAR-myum poo-roo-SHOSH-noo-tay / na cha sun-nya-sa-NAA-day-va SID-dhim sa-ma-dhi-GUCH-cha-ti
translation: Not by refusing to begin work does a person reach freedom from action, and not by renunciation alone does anyone arrive at perfection.
source: Bhagavad Gita 3.4, Sanskrit Wikisource contributors, CC BY-SA, https://sa.wikisource.org/wiki/%E0%A4%AD%E0%A4%97%E0%A4%B5%E0%A4%A6%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%97%E0%A5%80%E0%A4%A4%E0%A4%BE/%E0%A4%95%E0%A4%B0%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%AE%E0%A4%AF%E0%A5%8B%E0%A4%97%E0%A4%83; translation: Dharma Daily draft, pending review

words.meaning: by not undertaking, by never beginning
freedom from action, the actionless state
by renunciation, by giving works up

meaning: You cannot reach the state beyond action by simply not acting. Quitting your work is not the same as transcending it, and putting on the robes of renunciation does not by itself deliver the goal. The verse opens Krishna's case for karma yoga: the way past work runs through work done rightly, not around it. For daily practice, it names a familiar trap — mistaking avoidance for detachment. Skipping the hard task is not spiritual progress. Traditions read the destination differently: Advaita takes naishkarmya as the actionless stillness of Self-knowledge that disciplined action prepares the mind for, while Vishishtadvaita and Dvaita hold that action offered in devotion remains the path itself, with renunciation happening inwardly.
reflection: Where in your life are you calling avoidance "detachment" — and what would rightly-done action look like there instead?

devanagari: नियतं कुरु कर्म त्वं कर्म ज्यायो ह्यकर्मणः । / शरीरयात्रापि च ते न प्रसिद्ध्येदकर्मणः ॥3.8॥
iast: niyataṃ kuru karma tvaṃ karma jyāyo hyakarmaṇaḥ । / śarīrayātrāpi ca te na prasiddhyedakarmaṇaḥ ॥3.8॥
sayIt: ni-ya-TUM KOO-roo KAR-ma tvum KAR-ma JYAA-yo hya-KAR-ma-nah / sha-REE-ra-YAA-traa-pi cha tay na pra-SID-dhyay-da-KAR-ma-nah
translation: Do the work that is yours to do, for action is better than inaction; without action, even keeping your body going would be impossible.
source: Bhagavad Gita 3.8, Sanskrit Wikisource contributors, CC BY-SA, https://sa.wikisource.org/wiki/%E0%A4%AD%E0%A4%97%E0%A4%B5%E0%A4%A6%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%97%E0%A5%80%E0%A4%A4%E0%A4%BE/%E0%A4%95%E0%A4%B0%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%AE%E0%A4%AF%E0%A5%8B%E0%A4%97%E0%A4%83; translation: Dharma Daily draft, pending review

words.meaning: the upkeep of the body, bodily maintenance

meaning: Krishna makes the practical case against opting out: doing nothing is not actually available to you. Even staying alive — eating, moving, breathing — is action, so the choice is never between action and inaction, only between doing your allotted work and doing something lesser. For daily practice the verse is bracingly simple: identify the work that is genuinely yours today and do it, rather than drifting through substitute activity. Traditions differ on what "prescribed action" ultimately means — Advaita commentators emphasise ordained duties as purification that readies the mind for knowledge, while Vishishtadvaita and Dvaita read the same duties as ongoing worship offered to the Lord — but all agree the duty itself is not optional.
reflection: What is the one piece of work that is genuinely yours today, and what substitute activity are you tempted to do instead?

devanagari: यज्ञार्थात्कर्मणोऽन्यत्र लोकोऽयं कर्मबन्धनः । / तदर्थं कर्म कौन्तेय मुक्तसङ्गः समाचर ॥3.9॥
iast: yajñārthātkarmaṇo'nyatra loko'yaṃ karmabandhanaḥ । / tadarthaṃ karma kaunteya muktasaṅgaḥ samācara ॥3.9॥
sayIt: yug-YAAR-thaat kar-ma-NO-nya-tra lo-KO-yum KAR-ma-BUN-dha-nah / ta-DAR-thum KAR-ma kaun-TAY-ya mook-ta-SUN-gah sa-MAA-cha-ra
translation: Except for action done as sacrifice, this world is bound by action; so act for that purpose, son of Kunti, free from attachment.
source: Bhagavad Gita 3.9, Sanskrit Wikisource contributors, CC BY-SA, https://sa.wikisource.org/wiki/%E0%A4%AD%E0%A4%97%E0%A4%B5%E0%A4%A6%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%97%E0%A5%80%E0%A4%A4%E0%A4%BE/%E0%A4%95%E0%A4%B0%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%AE%E0%A4%AF%E0%A5%8B%E0%A4%97%E0%A4%83; translation: Dharma Daily draft, pending review

words.meaning: for the sake of sacrifice, of offering

meaning: Work binds — unless it is done as an offering. The same task can chain you or free you; what changes is not the task but its direction. Action performed as yajna, as sacrifice, escapes the machinery of accumulating karma because it is not done to feed the self. For daily practice this reframes ordinary work: the email, the cooking, the caregiving can each be turned into an offering by dropping the grasping and dedicating the act. Traditions read yajna differently — Advaita commentators take it broadly as duty done for the Lord and cosmic order as purification, while Vishishtadvaita and Dvaita read it pointedly as worship of Vishnu, every act offered to him — and both readings fit the verse.
reflection: Which ordinary task today could you perform as an offering rather than a transaction?

devanagari: एवं प्रवर्तितं चक्रं नानुवर्तयतीह यः । / अघायुरिन्द्रियारामो मोघं पार्थ स जीवति ॥3.16॥
iast: evaṃ pravartitaṃ cakraṃ nānuvartayatīha yaḥ । / aghāyurindriyārāmo moghaṃ pārtha sa jīvati ॥3.16॥
sayIt: AY-vum pra-var-TI-tum CHUK-rum naa-noo-var-ta-ya-TEE-ha yah / a-GHAA-yoor in-dri-YAA-raa-mo MO-ghum PAAR-tha sa JEE-va-ti
translation: One who does not help turn the wheel thus set in motion — living wrongly, absorbed in the senses — lives in vain, Partha.
source: Bhagavad Gita 3.16, Sanskrit Wikisource contributors, CC BY-SA, https://sa.wikisource.org/wiki/%E0%A4%AD%E0%A4%97%E0%A4%B5%E0%A4%A6%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%97%E0%A5%80%E0%A4%A4%E0%A4%BE/%E0%A4%95%E0%A4%B0%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%AE%E0%A4%AF%E0%A5%8B%E0%A4%97%E0%A4%83; translation: Dharma Daily draft, pending review

words.meaning: does not keep turning, does not follow along with
whose life is sinful, wrongly lived

meaning: The "wheel" is the cycle Krishna has just described: beings live on food, food comes from rain, rain from sacrifice, sacrifice from action — a circulation of mutual giving that sustains the world. To take from that cycle without contributing, living only for one's own pleasure, is to live pointlessly. For daily practice the verse asks a blunt question: are you a participant or only a consumer? Everyone receives constantly — from family, society, nature; the verse insists something must flow back. Commentators genuinely differ on the wheel's scope — some in the Advaita line stress the Vedic ritual cycle for those not yet renunciates, while theistic readings see the whole cosmic order of offering to the Lord — but none excuses free-riding.
reflection: Where are you drawing from the wheel — family, community, nature — without putting anything back?

devanagari: तस्मादसक्तः सततं कार्यं कर्म समाचर । / असक्तो ह्याचरन्कर्म परमाप्नोति पूरुषः ॥3.19॥
iast: tasmādasaktaḥ satataṃ kāryaṃ karma samācara । / asakto hyācarankarma paramāpnoti pūruṣaḥ ॥3.19॥
sayIt: tas-MAA-da-SUK-tah sa-ta-TUM KAAR-yum KAR-ma sa-MAA-cha-ra / a-SUK-to hyaa-cha-run KAR-ma pa-ra-MAAP-no-ti POO-roo-shah
translation: Therefore, always do the work that must be done, without attachment; for by acting unattached a person reaches the highest.
source: Bhagavad Gita 3.19, Sanskrit Wikisource contributors, CC BY-SA, https://sa.wikisource.org/wiki/%E0%A4%AD%E0%A4%97%E0%A4%B5%E0%A4%A6%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%97%E0%A5%80%E0%A4%A4%E0%A4%BE/%E0%A4%95%E0%A4%B0%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%AE%E0%A4%AF%E0%A5%8B%E0%A4%97%E0%A4%83; translation: Dharma Daily draft, pending review

words.meaning: that which ought to be done

meaning: This verse compresses karma yoga into one instruction: do what needs doing, constantly, without attachment — and that very practice carries you to the highest. Notice what it does not say: it does not lower the bar on effort or excuse careless work. Detachment applies to the clinging, not the quality. For daily practice it means the dishes, the deadline, and the difficult conversation are all "kāryam karma" — work that must be done — and each is an opportunity to practise doing it fully while holding it lightly. Traditions read "the highest" differently: Advaita takes unattached action as purifying the mind for liberating Self-knowledge, while Vishishtadvaita and Dvaita see it leading to attainment of the Lord himself — and the verse leaves room for both.
reflection: What must be done today that you could practise doing fully — and holding lightly?

devanagari: यद्यदाचरति श्रेष्ठस्तत्तदेवेतरो जनः । / स यत्प्रमाणं कुरुते लोकस्तदनुवर्तते ॥3.21॥
iast: yadyadācarati śreṣṭhastattadevetaro janaḥ । / sa yatpramāṇaṃ kurute lokastadanuvartate ॥3.21॥
sayIt: yud-ya-DAA-cha-ra-ti SHRAYSH-thus tat-ta-DAY-vay-ta-ro ja-nah / sa yat pra-MAA-num koo-roo-tay LO-kas ta-da-noo-VAR-ta-tay
translation: Whatever a great person does, other people do the same; whatever standard such a person sets, the world follows.
source: Bhagavad Gita 3.21, Sanskrit Wikisource contributors, CC BY-SA, https://sa.wikisource.org/wiki/%E0%A4%AD%E0%A4%97%E0%A4%B5%E0%A4%A6%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%97%E0%A5%80%E0%A4%A4%E0%A4%BE/%E0%A4%95%E0%A4%B0%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%AE%E0%A4%AF%E0%A5%8B%E0%A4%97%E0%A4%83; translation: Dharma Daily draft, pending review

words.meaning: the best person, the respected one

meaning: People do not follow instructions; they follow examples. Whoever is looked up to — a parent, a manager, an elder sibling, anyone with even a little standing — is quietly setting the standard others live by, whether or not they intend to. Krishna offers this as a reason to keep acting even after personal need has fallen away: your conduct is never only yours. For daily practice, it turns influence into responsibility — notice who watches you, and let that sharpen how you show up. Commentators across Advaita, Vishishtadvaita, and Dvaita read this verse in essentially the same way, as the foundation for lokasangraha, acting for the world's cohesion — a rare point of broad agreement.
reflection: Who quietly takes their standard from you, and what did your conduct teach them today?

devanagari: सक्ताः कर्मण्यविद्वांसो यथा कुर्वन्ति भारत । / कुर्याद्विद्वांस्तथासक्तश्चिकीर्षुर्लोकसंग्रहम् ॥3.25॥
iast: saktāḥ karmaṇyavidvāṃso yathā kurvanti bhārata । / kuryādvidvāṃstathāsaktaścikīrṣurlokasaṃgraham ॥3.25॥
sayIt: suk-TAAH kar-mun-ya-vid-VAAM-so ya-THAA koor-VUN-ti BHAA-ra-ta / koor-YAAD vid-VAAMS ta-THAA-suk-tush chi-KEER-shoor LO-ka-SUN-gra-hum
translation: As the unwise act, attached to their work, Bharata, so should the wise act — unattached, wishing to hold the world together.
source: Bhagavad Gita 3.25, Sanskrit Wikisource contributors, CC BY-SA, https://sa.wikisource.org/wiki/%E0%A4%AD%E0%A4%97%E0%A4%B5%E0%A4%A6%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%97%E0%A5%80%E0%A4%A4%E0%A4%BE/%E0%A4%95%E0%A4%B0%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%AE%E0%A4%AF%E0%A5%8B%E0%A4%97%E0%A4%83; translation: Dharma Daily draft, pending review

words.meaning: the holding-together, the welfare of the world

meaning: Watch how someone who deeply wants a result works: energetic, careful, thorough. Krishna says the wise should work with exactly that intensity — minus the clinging. Nothing about detachment licenses half-effort; the outward diligence stays identical, and only the inner motive changes, from personal gain to lokasangraha, holding the world together. For daily practice, this dissolves the excuse that spiritual maturity means caring less about doing things well. Traditions differ on who this "wise one" is — in Advaita, the knower has nothing left to gain and acts purely for the world's benefit, while Vishishtadvaita and Dvaita see even the realised soul continuing to act as loving service to the Lord — yet all agree the wise keep working.
reflection: If you kept today's effort exactly the same but changed the motive from personal gain to the good of those around you, what would shift?

devanagari: प्रकृतेः क्रियमाणानि गुणैः कर्माणि सर्वशः । / अहंकारविमूढात्मा कर्ताहमिति मन्यते ॥3.27॥
iast: prakṛteḥ kriyamāṇāni guṇaiḥ karmāṇi sarvaśaḥ । / ahaṃkāravimūḍhātmā kartāhamiti manyate ॥3.27॥
sayIt: pra-kri-TAYH kri-ya-MAA-naa-ni goo-NYE-hee kar-MAA-ni sar-va-SHAH / a-hung-KAA-ra-vi-MOO-dhaat-maa kar-TAA-ha-mi-ti MUN-ya-tay
translation: All actions are carried out by the gunas of nature; one whose mind is deluded by ego thinks, "I am the doer."
source: Bhagavad Gita 3.27, Sanskrit Wikisource contributors, CC BY-SA, https://sa.wikisource.org/wiki/%E0%A4%AD%E0%A4%97%E0%A4%B5%E0%A4%A6%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%97%E0%A5%80%E0%A4%A4%E0%A4%BE/%E0%A4%95%E0%A4%B0%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%AE%E0%A4%AF%E0%A5%8B%E0%A4%97%E0%A4%83; translation: Dharma Daily draft, pending review

words.meaning: by the gunas, the qualities of nature
one whose mind is deluded by ego

meaning: Every action you take runs on machinery you did not build — body, temperament, habit, circumstance, all of it the play of nature's gunas. The ego then steps in and signs its name to the finished work: "I did that." Krishna calls this signature the core delusion. For daily practice, the verse loosens the grip of both pride in success and crushing guilt in failure — much of what happens through you is nature moving. The schools genuinely divide here: Advaita holds the Self never acts at all, so all doership belongs to prakriti, while Vishishtadvaita and Dvaita maintain the soul is a real but dependent agent, and the error lies in claiming independent doership apart from nature and the Lord.
reflection: Think of something you are proud of or ashamed of from this week — how much of it was truly "you," and how much was nature moving through you?

devanagari: मयि सर्वाणि कर्माणि संन्यस्याध्यात्मचेतसा । / निराशीर्निर्ममो भूत्वा युध्यस्व विगतज्वरः ॥3.30॥
iast: mayi sarvāṇi karmāṇi saṃnyasyādhyātmacetasā । / nirāśīrnirmamo bhūtvā yudhyasva vigatajvaraḥ ॥3.30॥
sayIt: MA-yi sar-VAA-ni kar-MAA-ni sun-nyas-YAA-dhyaat-ma-CHAY-ta-saa / ni-RAA-sheer NEER-ma-mo BHOOT-vaa YOO-dhyas-va vi-ga-ta-JVA-rah
translation: Surrendering all actions to me, with mind resting in the Self, free of craving and possessiveness, fight — with the fever gone.
source: Bhagavad Gita 3.30, Sanskrit Wikisource contributors, CC BY-SA, https://sa.wikisource.org/wiki/%E0%A4%AD%E0%A4%97%E0%A4%B5%E0%A4%A6%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%97%E0%A5%80%E0%A4%A4%E0%A4%BE/%E0%A4%95%E0%A4%B0%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%AE%E0%A4%AF%E0%A5%8B%E0%A4%97%E0%A4%83; translation: Dharma Daily draft, pending review

words.meaning: with mind fixed on the Self, with inward awareness
with the fever gone, free of anguish

meaning: Krishna's instruction to Arjuna is startlingly complete: hand every action over to me, drop the craving and the "mine," and then — fight. Surrender here does not mean retreat from difficulty; it means entering the difficulty without the fever, the anxious inner burning that comes from carrying outcomes alone. For daily practice, whatever your battle is today — a diagnosis, a deadline, a conflict — the verse offers a sequence: offer it up first, release the grasping, then act wholeheartedly. Traditions read the surrender differently: Advaita commentators take it as casting actions on the Lord with the discernment that the Self is not the agent, while Vishishtadvaita and Dvaita hear a literal call to loving surrender of every act to Krishna as its true master.
reflection: What battle are you facing with a fever of anxiety — and what would it mean to offer it up before you fight it?

devanagari: श्रेयान्स्वधर्मो विगुणः परधर्मात्स्वनुष्ठितात् । / स्वधर्मे निधनं श्रेयः परधर्मो भयावहः ॥3.35॥
iast: śreyānsvadharmo viguṇaḥ paradharmātsvanuṣṭhitāt । / svadharme nidhanaṃ śreyaḥ paradharmo bhayāvahaḥ ॥3.35॥
sayIt: SHRAY-yaan sva-DHAR-mo vi-goo-NAH pa-ra-dhar-MAAT sva-noosh-thi-TAAT / sva-DHAR-may ni-dha-NUM SHRAY-yah pa-ra-DHAR-mo bha-YAA-va-hah
translation: Better your own dharma done imperfectly than another's dharma done well; better to die in your own dharma — another's dharma invites danger.
source: Bhagavad Gita 3.35, Sanskrit Wikisource contributors, CC BY-SA, https://sa.wikisource.org/wiki/%E0%A4%AD%E0%A4%97%E0%A4%B5%E0%A4%A6%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%97%E0%A5%80%E0%A4%A4%E0%A4%BE/%E0%A4%95%E0%A4%B0%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%AE%E0%A4%AF%E0%A5%8B%E0%A4%97%E0%A4%83; translation: Dharma Daily draft, pending review

words.meaning: one's own dharma, one's own duty

meaning: Doing your own work badly beats doing someone else's work brilliantly. The verse names a temptation everyone knows: another person's path always looks cleaner, easier, more rewarding than the flawed, unfinished one in front of you. Krishna's counsel is stark — stay on yours, even at cost — because a borrowed life, however polished, is built on ground that is not yours. For daily practice, it is a call to stop comparing and to work your own patch honestly. Traditions genuinely diverge on what svadharma means — duty tied to one's social station and stage of life in classical Advaita commentary, the discipline suited to one's embodied nature in Vishishtadvaita, or the calling given by the Lord to each soul's intrinsic nature in Dvaita — and none reads it as licence to disparage another's path.
reflection: Whose path have you been envying — and what would it look like to fully commit to your own imperfect one today?

devanagari: यदा यदा हि धर्मस्य ग्लानिर्भवति भारत । / अभ्युत्थानमधर्मस्य तदात्मानं सृजाम्यहम् ॥4.7॥
iast: yadā yadā hi dharmasya glānirbhavati bhārata । / abhyutthānamadharmasya tadātmānaṃ sṛjāmyaham ॥4.7॥
sayIt: ya-DAA ya-DAA hi DHAR-mas-ya GLAA-nir BHA-va-ti BHAA-ra-ta / abh-yoot-THAA-nam a-DHAR-mas-ya ta-DAAT-maa-nam sri-JAAM-ya-ham
translation: Whenever dharma declines and adharma rises, O Bharata, then I bring myself forth.
source: Bhagavad Gita 4.7, Sanskrit Wikisource contributors, CC BY-SA, https://sa.wikisource.org/wiki/%E0%A4%AD%E0%A4%97%E0%A4%B5%E0%A4%A6%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%97%E0%A5%80%E0%A4%A4%E0%A4%BE/%E0%A4%9C%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%9E%E0%A4%BE%E0%A4%A8%E0%A4%95%E0%A4%B0%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%AE%E0%A4%B8%E0%A4%82%E0%A4%A8%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%AF%E0%A4%BE%E0%A4%B8%E0%A4%AF%E0%A5%8B%E0%A4%97%E0%A4%83; translation: Dharma Daily draft, pending review
meaning: Krishna states the promise behind every avatar story: the divine does not stand back and watch dharma collapse. Whenever righteousness wanes and its opposite gains ground, the Lord acts — entering the world rather than abandoning it. The verse is famous as reassurance, but for daily practice it also sets a pattern to imitate: decline is answered by showing up, not by despair. When something you are responsible for starts slipping — a habit, a relationship, a standard at work — the dharmic response is presence and action. Traditions read the descent itself differently: Vaishnava schools such as Vishishtadvaita and Dvaita take the avatar as a real birth of a personal God, while Advaita reads it as the unborn absolute appearing through its own māyā — and this verse is a root text for both.
reflection: Where in your life is something quietly declining that is waiting for you to show up?

devanagari: परित्राणाय साधूनां विनाशाय च दुष्कृताम् । / धर्मसंस्थापनार्थाय सम्भवामि युगे युगे ॥4.8॥
iast: paritrāṇāya sādhūnāṃ vināśāya ca duṣkṛtām । / dharmasaṃsthāpanārthāya sambhavāmi yuge yuge ॥4.8॥
sayIt: pa-ri-TRAA-naa-ya saa-DHOO-naam vi-NAA-shaa-ya cha doosh-kri-TAAM / dhar-ma-sam-sthaa-pa-NAAR-thaa-ya sam-bha-VAA-mi yoo-GAY yoo-GAY
translation: To protect the good, to destroy evildoers, and to firmly establish dharma, I come into being age after age.
source: Bhagavad Gita 4.8, Sanskrit Wikisource contributors, CC BY-SA, https://sa.wikisource.org/wiki/%E0%A4%AD%E0%A4%97%E0%A4%B5%E0%A4%A6%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%97%E0%A5%80%E0%A4%A4%E0%A4%BE/%E0%A4%9C%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%9E%E0%A4%BE%E0%A4%A8%E0%A4%95%E0%A4%B0%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%AE%E0%A4%B8%E0%A4%82%E0%A4%A8%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%AF%E0%A4%BE%E0%A4%B8%E0%A4%AF%E0%A5%8B%E0%A4%97%E0%A4%83; translation: Dharma Daily draft, pending review

words.meaning: for the sake of firmly establishing dharma
I come into being, I take birth

meaning: The companion to 4.7, giving the threefold purpose of divine descent: shelter the good, end what does active harm, and set dharma back on firm footing. Notice the order — protection comes first. The verse is a promise of recurrence: yuge yuge, age after age, meaning the work of restoring dharma is never finished once and for all, and no age is beyond help. For daily practice, the three purposes make a usable checklist for your own actions: does this protect someone, does it stop a harm, does it steady something good? Schools diverge on the birth itself — Vishishtadvaita and Dvaita hold the Lord truly descends as a personal saviour, while Advaita reads the appearance as māyā over an unborn absolute — and the verse sustains both readings.
reflection: Which of the three — protecting the good, stopping a harm, steadying dharma — does today ask of you?

devanagari: ये यथा मां प्रपद्यन्ते तांस्तथैव भजाम्यहम् । / मम वर्त्मानुवर्तन्ते मनुष्याः पार्थ सर्वशः ॥4.11॥
iast: ye yathā māṃ prapadyante tāṃstathaiva bhajāmyaham । / mama vartmānuvartante manuṣyāḥ pārtha sarvaśaḥ ॥4.11॥
sayIt: yay ya-THAA maam pra-PAD-yan-tay taams ta-THAI-va bha-JAAM-ya-ham / MA-ma vart-MAA-noo-var-TAN-tay ma-NOOSH-yaah PAAR-tha SAR-va-shah
translation: In whatever way people approach me, in that very way I receive them; all humans, O Partha, follow my path in every way.
source: Bhagavad Gita 4.11, Sanskrit Wikisource contributors, CC BY-SA, https://sa.wikisource.org/wiki/%E0%A4%AD%E0%A4%97%E0%A4%B5%E0%A4%A6%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%97%E0%A5%80%E0%A4%A4%E0%A4%BE/%E0%A4%9C%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%9E%E0%A4%BE%E0%A4%A8%E0%A4%95%E0%A4%B0%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%AE%E0%A4%B8%E0%A4%82%E0%A4%A8%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%AF%E0%A4%BE%E0%A4%B8%E0%A4%AF%E0%A5%8B%E0%A4%97%E0%A4%83; translation: Dharma Daily draft, pending review

words.meaning: in every way, on every side

meaning: A verse of reciprocity: the divine meets people in the manner they come. Approach with love, and love is what answers; approach seeking knowledge, and knowledge opens; approach with a small, distracted offering, and even that is not turned away. Nothing forced, nothing rationed — the shape of the relationship is set by the seeker's own approach. For daily practice, this removes the excuse of not being ready enough: come as you are, in whatever mode is honest today. Commentators do diverge on the second line's reach — Advaita tends to read all worship as ultimately reaching one reality, while Vishishtadvaita and Dvaita read the Lord personally rewarding each devotee's chosen mode of approach — and both readings keep the verse's generosity intact.
reflection: If the divine meets you exactly as you approach — how are you approaching today?

devanagari: कर्मण्यकर्म यः पश्येदकर्मणि च कर्म यः । / स बुद्धिमान्मनुष्येषु स युक्तः कृत्स्नकर्मकृत् ॥4.18॥
iast: karmaṇyakarma yaḥ paśyedakarmaṇi ca karma yaḥ । / sa buddhimānmanuṣyeṣu sa yuktaḥ kṛtsnakarmakṛt ॥4.18॥
sayIt: kar-MUN-ya-KAR-ma yah PASH-yed a-KAR-ma-ni cha KAR-ma yah / sa bood-dhi-MAAN ma-noosh-YAY-shoo sa YOOK-tah krits-na-KAR-ma-krit
translation: One who sees inaction in action, and action in inaction, is wise among humans; that one is a yogi who has accomplished all action.
source: Bhagavad Gita 4.18, Sanskrit Wikisource contributors, CC BY-SA, https://sa.wikisource.org/wiki/%E0%A4%AD%E0%A4%97%E0%A4%B5%E0%A4%A6%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%97%E0%A5%80%E0%A4%A4%E0%A4%BE/%E0%A4%9C%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%9E%E0%A4%BE%E0%A4%A8%E0%A4%95%E0%A4%B0%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%AE%E0%A4%B8%E0%A4%82%E0%A4%A8%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%AF%E0%A4%BE%E0%A4%B8%E0%A4%AF%E0%A5%8B%E0%A4%97%E0%A4%83; translation: Dharma Daily draft, pending review

words.meaning: doer of all action, one whose work is complete

meaning: A deliberate riddle. Seeing inaction in action means acting fully while inwardly free — no clinging, no ego claiming "I did this," so the action leaves no binding residue. Seeing action in inaction means recognising that refusing to act is itself a choice with consequences: sitting out is still a move, and often a costly one. The wise person is fooled by neither — not by busyness that is really avoidance, nor by stillness that is really abdication. For daily practice, apply both tests: in your effort, is there grasping? In your restraint, is there hiding? Krishna calls the one who sees this clearly the true doer of all action.
reflection: Is there something you are calling patience or restraint that is actually a decision you are avoiding?

devanagari: श्रेयान्द्रव्यमयाद्यज्ञाज्ज्ञानयज्ञः परन्तप । / सर्वं कर्माखिलं पार्थ ज्ञाने परिसमाप्यते ॥4.33॥
iast: śreyāndravyamayādyajñājjñānayajñaḥ parantapa । / sarvaṃ karmākhilaṃ pārtha jñāne parisamāpyate ॥4.33॥
sayIt: SHRAY-yaan drav-ya-ma-YAAD yag-YAAJ gyaa-na-YAG-yah pa-ran-TA-pa / SAR-vam kar-MAA-khi-lam PAAR-tha GYAA-nay pa-ri-sa-MAAP-ya-tay
translation: Better than the sacrifice of material things is the sacrifice of knowledge, O scorcher of foes; all action without exception, O Partha, culminates in knowledge.
source: Bhagavad Gita 4.33, Sanskrit Wikisource contributors, CC BY-SA, https://sa.wikisource.org/wiki/%E0%A4%AD%E0%A4%97%E0%A4%B5%E0%A4%A6%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%97%E0%A5%80%E0%A4%A4%E0%A4%BE/%E0%A4%9C%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%9E%E0%A4%BE%E0%A4%A8%E0%A4%95%E0%A4%B0%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%AE%E0%A4%B8%E0%A4%82%E0%A4%A8%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%AF%E0%A4%BE%E0%A4%B8%E0%A4%AF%E0%A5%8B%E0%A4%97%E0%A4%83; translation: Dharma Daily draft, pending review

words.meaning: than that made of material things

meaning: After listing many kinds of sacrifice — offerings of wealth, austerity, breath, study — Krishna ranks them: the offering made in knowledge outweighs any offering of things. Not because giving things is wrong, but because outer ritual finds its purpose in inner understanding; all action, without exception, ripens into knowledge. For daily practice, this reorders effort. Doing more is not automatically better than understanding why you do it. Bring understanding into the act — know what your work is for, what your worship means, what your giving serves — and the same action becomes a higher sacrifice. Ritual done blindly stays external; ritual done knowingly transforms the one performing it.
reflection: What is one routine you perform on autopilot that would change if you remembered why you do it?

devanagari: तद्विद्धि प्रणिपातेन परिप्रश्नेन सेवया । / उपदेक्ष्यन्ति ते ज्ञानं ज्ञानिनस्तत्त्वदर्शिनः ॥4.34॥
iast: tadviddhi praṇipātena paripraśnena sevayā । / upadekṣyanti te jñānaṃ jñāninastattvadarśinaḥ ॥4.34॥
sayIt: tad-VID-dhi pra-ni-PAA-tay-na pa-ri-PRASH-nay-na SAY-va-yaa / oo-pa-DEK-shyan-ti tay GYAA-nam GYAA-ni-nas tat-tva-DAR-shi-nah
translation: Learn that knowledge by bowing, by sincere questioning, and by service; the wise who have seen the truth will teach it to you.
source: Bhagavad Gita 4.34, Sanskrit Wikisource contributors, CC BY-SA, https://sa.wikisource.org/wiki/%E0%A4%AD%E0%A4%97%E0%A4%B5%E0%A4%A6%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%97%E0%A5%80%E0%A4%A4%E0%A4%BE/%E0%A4%9C%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%9E%E0%A4%BE%E0%A4%A8%E0%A4%95%E0%A4%B0%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%AE%E0%A4%B8%E0%A4%82%E0%A4%A8%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%AF%E0%A4%BE%E0%A4%B8%E0%A4%AF%E0%A5%8B%E0%A4%97%E0%A4%83; translation: Dharma Daily draft, pending review
meaning: The classic verse on how spiritual knowledge is actually transmitted. Krishna gives three requirements, and all three are attitudes of the student, not qualifications of the teacher: humility (bowing — being teachable), inquiry (asking real questions, not performing knowledge), and service (staying long enough, and giving enough, for trust to form). Notice the verse does not say knowledge is downloaded; it says the truth-seers will teach you when approached this way. For daily practice: pick your teachers carefully — the standard here is that they have seen the truth, not that they are popular — and then check your own posture. Arrogance closes the very door that questions are meant to open.
reflection: Whom do you trust enough to ask a real question — and when did you last actually ask one?

devanagari: अपि चेदसि पापेभ्यः सर्वेभ्यः पापकृत्तमः । / सर्वं ज्ञानप्लवेनैव वृजिनं सन्तरिष्यसि ॥4.36॥
iast: api cedasi pāpebhyaḥ sarvebhyaḥ pāpakṛttamaḥ । / sarvaṃ jñānaplavenaiva vṛjinaṃ santariṣyasi ॥4.36॥
sayIt: A-pi CHED a-si paa-PAY-bhyah sar-VAY-bhyah paa-pa-KRIT-ta-mah / SAR-vam gyaa-na-pla-VAY-nai-va vri-JI-nam san-ta-RISH-ya-si
translation: Even if you were the most sinful of all sinners, you would cross over all wrongdoing by the boat of knowledge alone.
source: Bhagavad Gita 4.36, Sanskrit Wikisource contributors, CC BY-SA, https://sa.wikisource.org/wiki/%E0%A4%AD%E0%A4%97%E0%A4%B5%E0%A4%A6%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%97%E0%A5%80%E0%A4%A4%E0%A4%BE/%E0%A4%9C%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%9E%E0%A4%BE%E0%A4%A8%E0%A4%95%E0%A4%B0%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%AE%E0%A4%B8%E0%A4%82%E0%A4%A8%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%AF%E0%A4%BE%E0%A4%B8%E0%A4%AF%E0%A5%8B%E0%A4%97%E0%A4%83; translation: Dharma Daily draft, pending review
meaning: One of the Gita's most hopeful verses. Krishna takes the extreme case on purpose — even the worst wrongdoer of all — and says the boat of knowledge still carries that person across. The image matters: a flood of past mistakes is not drained away drop by drop; it is crossed, in a vessel, once you climb in. No one is disqualified by their history. For daily practice, this cuts against the paralysis of guilt: the response to having done wrong is not endless self-punishment but honest understanding — seeing clearly what you did, why, and who you actually are beneath the act. Regret that leads to knowledge becomes a boat; regret that only circles becomes the flood.
reflection: What past mistake are you still treading water in, instead of building the understanding that would carry you across?

devanagari: न हि ज्ञानेन सदृशं पवित्रमिह विद्यते । / तत्स्वयं योगसंसिद्धः कालेनात्मनि विन्दति ॥4.38॥
iast: na hi jñānena sadṛśaṃ pavitramiha vidyate । / tatsvayaṃ yogasaṃsiddhaḥ kālenātmani vindati ॥4.38॥
sayIt: na hi gyaa-NAY-na sa-DRI-sham pa-VIT-ram i-ha VID-ya-tay / tat SVA-yam yo-ga-sam-SID-dhah kaa-LAY-naat-ma-ni VIN-da-ti
translation: Nothing in this world purifies like knowledge; one perfected through yoga finds it, in time, within oneself.
source: Bhagavad Gita 4.38, Sanskrit Wikisource contributors, CC BY-SA, https://sa.wikisource.org/wiki/%E0%A4%AD%E0%A4%97%E0%A4%B5%E0%A4%A6%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%97%E0%A5%80%E0%A4%A4%E0%A4%BE/%E0%A4%9C%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%9E%E0%A4%BE%E0%A4%A8%E0%A4%95%E0%A4%B0%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%AE%E0%A4%B8%E0%A4%82%E0%A4%A8%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%AF%E0%A4%BE%E0%A4%B8%E0%A4%AF%E0%A5%8B%E0%A4%97%E0%A4%83; translation: Dharma Daily draft, pending review
meaning: Two claims in one verse. First: of everything that purifies — rivers, rituals, austerities — nothing equals knowledge, because knowledge cleans the root where confusion lives, not just the surface. Second, and easy to miss: this knowledge is found within oneself, in time, by one ripened through practice. It is not handed over finished; the teacher points (as 4.34 says), but the finding happens inside, and it has a season. For daily practice, both halves matter — keep practising even when nothing seems to be happening, and stop expecting insight on demand. Kālena, "in time," is Krishna's own patience clause: steady discipline now, discovery when you are ready.
reflection: Where are you demanding instant clarity from a practice that is quietly working on its own schedule?

devanagari: श्रद्धावाँल्लभते ज्ञानं तत्परः संयतेन्द्रियः । / ज्ञानं लब्ध्वा परां शान्तिमचिरेणाधिगच्छति ॥4.39॥
iast: śraddhāvām̐llabhate jñānaṃ tatparaḥ saṃyatendriyaḥ । / jñānaṃ labdhvā parāṃ śāntimacireṇādhigacchati ॥4.39॥
sayIt: shrad-DHAA-vaan LA-bha-tay GYAA-nam TAT-pa-rah sam-ya-TEN-dri-yah / GYAA-nam LAB-dhvaa pa-RAAM SHAAN-tim a-chi-RAY-naa-dhi-GACH-cha-ti
translation: The person of faith, devoted to it, with senses restrained, gains knowledge; having gained knowledge, one soon reaches the highest peace.
source: Bhagavad Gita 4.39, Sanskrit Wikisource contributors, CC BY-SA, https://sa.wikisource.org/wiki/%E0%A4%AD%E0%A4%97%E0%A4%B5%E0%A4%A6%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%97%E0%A5%80%E0%A4%A4%E0%A4%BE/%E0%A4%9C%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%9E%E0%A4%BE%E0%A4%A8%E0%A4%95%E0%A4%B0%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%AE%E0%A4%B8%E0%A4%82%E0%A4%A8%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%AF%E0%A4%BE%E0%A4%B8%E0%A4%AF%E0%A5%8B%E0%A4%97%E0%A4%83; translation: Dharma Daily draft, pending review

words.meaning: devoted to it, intent on it

meaning: Krishna gives the recipe in order: faith, commitment, restraint — then knowledge — then peace. Faith (shraddha) here is not blind belief but working trust, the willingness to take the teaching seriously enough to test it in your own life. Commitment means making it your priority rather than a hobby; restraint of the senses means not letting every passing pull scatter the effort. Given those three, knowledge comes — and once knowledge comes, the verse promises, peace follows without long delay. For daily practice, notice what the sequence rules out: peace is not chased directly. Chase understanding with trust and steadiness, and peace arrives as the by-product it was always meant to be.
reflection: Which of the three — trust, commitment, or restraint — is the weakest link in your practice right now?

devanagari: तस्मादज्ञानसम्भूतं हृत्स्थं ज्ञानासिनात्मनः । / छित्त्वैनं संशयं योगमातिष्ठोत्तिष्ठ भारत ॥4.42॥
iast: tasmādajñānasambhūtaṃ hṛtsthaṃ jñānāsinātmanaḥ । / chittvainaṃ saṃśayaṃ yogamātiṣṭhottiṣṭha bhārata ॥4.42॥
sayIt: tas-MAAD ag-yaa-na-sam-BHOO-tam HRIT-stham gyaa-NAA-si-NAAT-ma-nah / chit-TVAI-nam san-SHA-yam YO-gam aa-TISH-thot-TISH-tha BHAA-ra-ta
translation: Therefore, with the sword of knowledge cut this doubt of yours, born of ignorance and seated in the heart; take your stand in yoga and arise, O Bharata.
source: Bhagavad Gita 4.42, Sanskrit Wikisource contributors, CC BY-SA, https://sa.wikisource.org/wiki/%E0%A4%AD%E0%A4%97%E0%A4%B5%E0%A4%A6%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%97%E0%A5%80%E0%A4%A4%E0%A4%BE/%E0%A4%9C%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%9E%E0%A4%BE%E0%A4%A8%E0%A4%95%E0%A4%B0%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%AE%E0%A4%B8%E0%A4%82%E0%A4%A8%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%AF%E0%A4%BE%E0%A4%B8%E0%A4%AF%E0%A5%8B%E0%A4%97%E0%A4%83; translation: Dharma Daily draft, pending review
meaning: The closing verse of chapter four, and it ends in two commands: cut, then rise. The doubt Krishna targets is not honest inquiry — the whole chapter has encouraged questions — but the corrosive, heart-lodged hesitation born of ignorance, the kind that keeps you circling instead of acting. Its remedy is a sword, and the sword is knowledge: doubt of this kind is not soothed away, it is cut through by understanding clearly enough to decide. And then the verse refuses to let clarity stay theoretical — uttiṣṭha, stand up. For daily practice: when a decision has been examined enough, further deliberation is just doubt wearing a thoughtful mask. Cut it, take your stand, and move.
reflection: What decision have you already examined enough — and what would standing up on it look like today?

devanagari: ज्ञेयः स नित्यसंन्यासी यो न द्वेष्टि न काङ्क्षति । / निर्द्वन्द्वो हि महाबाहो सुखं बन्धात्प्रमुच्यते ॥5.3॥
iast: jñeyaḥ sa nityasaṃnyāsī yo na dveṣṭi na kāṅkṣati । / nirdvandvo hi mahābāho sukhaṃ bandhātpramucyate ॥5.3॥
sayIt: GYAY-yah sa nit-ya-sun-NYAA-see yo na DVESH-ti na KAANK-sha-ti / nir-DVUN-dvo hi ma-haa-BAA-ho SU-khum bun-DHAAT pra-MOOCH-ya-tay
translation: Know that person as a perpetual renunciant who neither hates nor craves; free from the pairs of opposites, O mighty-armed one, they are easily released from bondage.
source: Bhagavad Gita 5.3, Sanskrit Wikisource contributors, CC BY-SA, https://sa.wikisource.org/wiki/%E0%A4%AD%E0%A4%97%E0%A4%B5%E0%A4%A6%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%97%E0%A5%80%E0%A4%A4%E0%A4%BE/%E0%A4%95%E0%A4%B0%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%AE%E0%A4%B8%E0%A4%82%E0%A4%A8%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%AF%E0%A4%BE%E0%A4%B8%E0%A4%AF%E0%A5%8B%E0%A4%97%E0%A4%83; translation: Dharma Daily draft, pending review

words.meaning: free from the pairs of opposites

meaning: Renunciation, Krishna says here, is not a costume or an address — it is the absence of two inner pulls. The person who neither hates what is in front of them nor aches for what is not is already a renunciant, whatever their outward life looks like. "Pairs of opposites" means the seesaw we live on: gain and loss, praise and blame, comfort and discomfort. Step off the seesaw and release comes easily, not through strain. For daily practice, notice the two pulls as they arise — aversion and craving — and name them. Commentators broadly agree on this verse's plain sense; Advaita, Vishishtadvaita, and Dvaita teachers alike treat it as praise of inner, not merely outward, renunciation.
reflection: Where in today's plans are you quietly hating one outcome and craving another — and what would it feel like to hold both loosely?

devanagari: ब्रह्मण्याधाय कर्माणि सङ्गं त्यक्त्वा करोति यः । / लिप्यते न स पापेन पद्मपत्रमिवाम्भसा ॥5.10॥
iast: brahmaṇyādhāya karmāṇi saṅgaṃ tyaktvā karoti yaḥ । / lipyate na sa pāpena padmapatramivāmbhasā ॥5.10॥
sayIt: brah-mun-YAA-dhaa-ya kar-MAA-ni SUN-gum tyukt-VAA ka-RO-ti yah / LIP-ya-tay na sa paa-PAY-na pud-ma-PUT-rum i-VAAM-bha-saa
translation: One who acts with attachment abandoned, placing all actions in Brahman, is untouched by sin, as a lotus leaf is untouched by water.
source: Bhagavad Gita 5.10, Sanskrit Wikisource contributors, CC BY-SA, https://sa.wikisource.org/wiki/%E0%A4%AD%E0%A4%97%E0%A4%B5%E0%A4%A6%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%97%E0%A5%80%E0%A4%A4%E0%A4%BE/%E0%A4%95%E0%A4%B0%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%AE%E0%A4%B8%E0%A4%82%E0%A4%A8%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%AF%E0%A4%BE%E0%A4%B8%E0%A4%AF%E0%A5%8B%E0%A4%97%E0%A4%83; translation: Dharma Daily draft, pending review
meaning: The lotus leaf grows in water, is splashed by water constantly, and stays dry — droplets bead up and roll off. That is the image for working in the world without being stained by it. The instruction has two parts: hand the action over — place it in the Divine rather than in your ego's account — and drop the clinging. You still act, fully and well; what changes is whose project it is. For daily practice, begin one piece of work today as an offering rather than a self-advancement. Traditions read "placing actions in Brahman" differently — Advaita commentators often gloss it as acting for Ishvara without claiming doership, while Vishishtadvaita and Dvaita read it as entrusting all action to the personal Lord — and both readings fit the verse.
reflection: What is one task you could do today as an offering, letting both the credit and the blame roll off like water from a lotus leaf?

devanagari: ज्ञानेन तु तदज्ञानं येषां नाशितमात्मनः । / तेषामादित्यवज्ज्ञानं प्रकाशयति तत्परम् ॥5.16॥
iast: jñānena tu tadajñānaṃ yeṣāṃ nāśitamātmanaḥ । / teṣāmādityavajjñānaṃ prakāśayati tatparam ॥5.16॥
sayIt: gyaa-NAY-na tu tud ug-YAA-num YAY-shaam NAA-shi-tum AAT-ma-nah / TAY-shaam aa-DIT-ya-vuj GYAA-num pra-KAA-sha-ya-ti tut PA-rum
translation: But for those in whom that ignorance of the self is destroyed by knowledge, their knowledge, like the sun, lights up the Supreme.
source: Bhagavad Gita 5.16, Sanskrit Wikisource contributors, CC BY-SA, https://sa.wikisource.org/wiki/%E0%A4%AD%E0%A4%97%E0%A4%B5%E0%A4%A6%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%97%E0%A5%80%E0%A4%A4%E0%A4%BE/%E0%A4%95%E0%A4%B0%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%AE%E0%A4%B8%E0%A4%82%E0%A4%A8%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%AF%E0%A4%BE%E0%A4%B8%E0%A4%AF%E0%A5%8B%E0%A4%97%E0%A4%83; translation: Dharma Daily draft, pending review
meaning: The previous verse says ignorance covers our knowledge the way a cloud covers the sky; this one describes the cloud burning off. Nothing new has to be manufactured — when the misunderstanding about who we are is removed, knowledge does what the sun does at dawn: it simply shines, and the highest truth stands revealed. The work is subtraction, not addition. For daily practice, treat learning about the self less like acquiring and more like clearing — one honest look at one assumption. Traditions differ on what the sun reveals: Advaita reads "that Supreme" as the one Self identical with Brahman, while Vishishtadvaita and Dvaita read it as the Lord known clearly by a purified soul that remains distinct — and each school reads the verse consistently within its own frame.
reflection: What is one assumption about yourself you could bring into the light today instead of leaving it in the dark?

devanagari: विद्याविनयसंपन्ने ब्राह्मणे गवि हस्तिनि । / शुनि चैव श्वपाके च पण्डिताः समदर्शिनः ॥5.18॥
iast: vidyāvinayasaṃpanne brāhmaṇe gavi hastini । / śuni caiva śvapāke ca paṇḍitāḥ samadarśinaḥ ॥5.18॥
sayIt: vid-YAA-vi-na-ya-sum-PUN-nay BRAAH-ma-nay GU-vi HUS-ti-ni / SHU-ni CHAI-va shva-PAA-kay cha PUN-di-taah sa-ma-DAR-shi-nah
translation: The wise look with an equal eye upon a brahmin endowed with learning and humility, a cow, an elephant, a dog, and an outcaste.
source: Bhagavad Gita 5.18, Sanskrit Wikisource contributors, CC BY-SA, https://sa.wikisource.org/wiki/%E0%A4%AD%E0%A4%97%E0%A4%B5%E0%A4%A6%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%97%E0%A5%80%E0%A4%A4%E0%A4%BE/%E0%A4%95%E0%A4%B0%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%AE%E0%A4%B8%E0%A4%82%E0%A4%A8%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%AF%E0%A4%BE%E0%A4%B8%E0%A4%AF%E0%A5%8B%E0%A4%97%E0%A4%83; translation: Dharma Daily draft, pending review

words.meaning: in an outcaste (literally "dog-cooker," the lowest social rank of the time)
seeing the same, with equal vision

meaning: The verse deliberately runs from the most honoured figure of its society to the most despised, adding two animals in between, and says the wise see the same in all of them. Bodies, ranks, and species differ wildly; what dwells within does not differ in worth. This is sama-darshana — equal vision — and the Gita treats it as a mark of real knowledge, not mere politeness. For daily practice, catch yourself mid-ranking: the person you defer to and the person you overlook. Traditions genuinely diverge on what exactly is equal: Advaita sees one identical Self in all, Vishishtadvaita sees selves alike in essence though embodied differently, and Dvaita sees distinct souls each equally indwelt by the Lord — the verse leaves room for each reading.
reflection: Who did you look past or quietly rank beneath you today, and what changes if you look again with an equal eye?

devanagari: न प्रहृष्येत्प्रियं प्राप्य नोद्विजेत्प्राप्य चाप्रियम् । / स्थिरबुद्धिरसंमूढो ब्रह्मविद्ब्रह्मणि स्थितः ॥5.20॥
iast: na prahṛṣyetpriyaṃ prāpya nodvijetprāpya cāpriyam । / sthirabuddhirasaṃmūḍho brahmavidbrahmaṇi sthitaḥ ॥5.20॥
sayIt: na pra-HRISH-yet PRI-yum PRAAP-ya nod-VI-jet PRAAP-ya CHAAP-ri-yum / sthi-ra-BUD-dhir a-sum-MOO-dho BRAH-ma-vid BRAH-ma-ni STHI-tah
translation: One should not exult on gaining the pleasant, nor be shaken on meeting the unpleasant; with steady understanding and free of delusion, the knower of Brahman stands established in Brahman.
source: Bhagavad Gita 5.20, Sanskrit Wikisource contributors, CC BY-SA, https://sa.wikisource.org/wiki/%E0%A4%AD%E0%A4%97%E0%A4%B5%E0%A4%A6%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%97%E0%A5%80%E0%A4%A4%E0%A4%BE/%E0%A4%95%E0%A4%B0%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%AE%E0%A4%B8%E0%A4%82%E0%A4%A8%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%AF%E0%A4%BE%E0%A4%B8%E0%A4%AF%E0%A5%8B%E0%A4%97%E0%A4%83; translation: Dharma Daily draft, pending review
meaning: Good news and bad news arrive all day, and each one tries to move you off your foundation — the win inflates you, the setback rattles you. This verse describes someone whose footing does not depend on the news at all, because it rests on something that does not fluctuate. It is not asking for numbness; delight and disappointment can be felt without becoming your address. For daily practice, when the next piece of news lands, notice the lurch — up or down — and take one breath before you move. Traditions agree on the steadiness while describing its ground differently: Advaita as abiding in the one Self, Vishishtadvaita and Dvaita as the stability of a soul anchored in the Lord.
reflection: What news — good or bad — are you bracing for right now, and could you meet either kind without losing your footing?

devanagari: ये हि संस्पर्शजा भोगा दुःखयोनय एव ते । / आद्यन्तवन्तः कौन्तेय न तेषु रमते बुधः ॥5.22॥
iast: ye hi saṃsparśajā bhogā duḥkhayonaya eva te । / ādyantavantaḥ kaunteya na teṣu ramate budhaḥ ॥5.22॥
sayIt: yay hi sum-spar-sha-JAA BHO-gaa DUH-kha-YO-na-ya AY-va tay / aad-YUN-ta-vun-tah kown-TAY-ya na TAY-shoo RA-ma-tay BU-dhah
translation: The enjoyments born of contact with the senses are truly wombs of sorrow; they have a beginning and an end, O son of Kunti — the wise take no delight in them.
source: Bhagavad Gita 5.22, Sanskrit Wikisource contributors, CC BY-SA, https://sa.wikisource.org/wiki/%E0%A4%AD%E0%A4%97%E0%A4%B5%E0%A4%A6%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%97%E0%A5%80%E0%A4%A4%E0%A4%BE/%E0%A4%95%E0%A4%B0%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%AE%E0%A4%B8%E0%A4%82%E0%A4%A8%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%AF%E0%A4%BE%E0%A4%B8%E0%A4%AF%E0%A5%8B%E0%A4%97%E0%A4%83; translation: Dharma Daily draft, pending review

words.meaning: born of contact (of the senses with their objects)
wombs of sorrow, sources of suffering
having a beginning and an end

meaning: The verse's diagnosis is structural, not moralising. Any pleasure that comes from contact — sense meeting object — has a start and therefore a stop, and everything with a stop carries its own ending inside it, like a womb carries a birth. The pleasure is not evil; it is simply unreliable, and building your happiness on it means building on something scheduled to leave. The wise are not joyless; they just stop banking on the unstable. For daily practice, watch one habitual pleasure today from start to finish and notice where the enjoyment actually ends. Commentators across Advaita, Vishishtadvaita, and Dvaita read this verse in essentially the same way — a shared warning, not a point of dispute.
reflection: Which pleasure do you keep returning to even though you already know exactly how it ends?

devanagari: शक्नोतीहैव यः सोढुं प्राक्शरीरविमोक्षणात् । / कामक्रोधोद्भवं वेगं स युक्तः स सुखी नरः ॥5.23॥
iast: śaknotīhaiva yaḥ soḍhuṃ prākśarīravimokṣaṇāt । / kāmakrodhodbhavaṃ vegaṃ sa yuktaḥ sa sukhī naraḥ ॥5.23॥
sayIt: shak-NO-tee-HAI-va yah SO-dhum praak sha-REE-ra-vi-MOK-sha-naat / kaa-ma-kro-DHOD-bha-vum VAY-gum sa YUK-tah sa su-KHEE na-rah
translation: One who can withstand, right here before leaving the body, the surge born of desire and anger — that person is a yogi, and that person is happy.
source: Bhagavad Gita 5.23, Sanskrit Wikisource contributors, CC BY-SA, https://sa.wikisource.org/wiki/%E0%A4%AD%E0%A4%97%E0%A4%B5%E0%A4%A6%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%97%E0%A5%80%E0%A4%A4%E0%A4%BE/%E0%A4%95%E0%A4%B0%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%AE%E0%A4%B8%E0%A4%82%E0%A4%A8%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%AF%E0%A4%BE%E0%A4%B8%E0%A4%AF%E0%A5%8B%E0%A4%97%E0%A4%83; translation: Dharma Daily draft, pending review

words.meaning: right here, in this very life
that one is yoked, established in yoga

meaning: The word vega means a surge — a flood tide, a rush. Desire and anger do not arrive politely; they arrive as force, and the verse is precise about the practice: not never feeling the surge, but being able to withstand it, here, now, while alive, without being swept into action. Two things get promised to whoever manages it: they are a yogi — this counts as real yoga, not just the seated kind — and they are happy, because a person carried off by every surge is never at rest. For daily practice, the whole art is the gap between feeling and acting. Advaita, Vishishtadvaita, and Dvaita teachers alike prize this restraint; the verse itself is not a point of doctrinal dispute.
reflection: When desire or anger last surged in you, what happened in the space between feeling it and acting on it?

devanagari: योऽन्तःसुखोऽन्तरारामस्तथान्तर्ज्योतिरेव यः । / स योगी ब्रह्मनिर्वाणं ब्रह्मभूतोऽधिगच्छति ॥5.24॥
iast: yo'ntaḥsukho'ntarārāmastathāntarjyotireva yaḥ । / sa yogī brahmanirvāṇaṃ brahmabhūto'dhigacchati ॥5.24॥
sayIt: yon-tah-SU-kho un-ta-RAA-raa-mus ta-THAAN-tar-JYO-tir AY-va yah / sa YO-gee brah-ma-nir-VAA-num brah-ma-BHOO-to dhi-GUCH-chha-ti
translation: The one whose happiness is within, whose delight is within, and whose light is within — that yogi, having become one with Brahman, attains the stillness of Brahman.
source: Bhagavad Gita 5.24, Sanskrit Wikisource contributors, CC BY-SA, https://sa.wikisource.org/wiki/%E0%A4%AD%E0%A4%97%E0%A4%B5%E0%A4%A6%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%97%E0%A5%80%E0%A4%A4%E0%A4%BE/%E0%A4%95%E0%A4%B0%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%AE%E0%A4%B8%E0%A4%82%E0%A4%A8%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%AF%E0%A4%BE%E0%A4%B8%E0%A4%AF%E0%A5%8B%E0%A4%97%E0%A4%83; translation: Dharma Daily draft, pending review

words.meaning: whose delight, whose resting place, is within
having become Brahman, absorbed in Brahman

meaning: Three times the verse says "within": happiness within, delight within, light within. It is describing someone whose sources have moved indoors — who no longer needs the day to go well, the room to approve, or circumstances to supply the glow. Such a person is not withdrawn from the world; they simply are not billing the world for their contentment. The reward named is brahma-nirvana, a settled stillness in the Divine. For daily practice, ask where you are currently outsourcing your mood, and reclaim one small piece of it. Traditions diverge honestly on "having become Brahman": Advaita reads it as realising identity with Brahman, while Vishishtadvaita and Dvaita read it as the soul reaching its purified, Brahman-like nature while remaining distinct from the Lord.
reflection: What would today look like if you drew your contentment from within instead of waiting for it to be delivered?

devanagari: लभन्ते ब्रह्मनिर्वाणमृषयः क्षीणकल्मषाः । / छिन्नद्वैधा यतात्मानः सर्वभूतहिते रताः ॥5.25॥
iast: labhante brahmanirvāṇamṛṣayaḥ kṣīṇakalmaṣāḥ । / chinnadvaidhā yatātmānaḥ sarvabhūtahite ratāḥ ॥5.25॥
sayIt: la-BHUN-tay brah-ma-nir-VAA-num RI-sha-yah KSHEE-na-KUL-ma-shaah / chhin-na-DVAI-dhaa ya-TAAT-maa-nah sar-va-BHOO-ta-hi-tay ra-TAAH
translation: The seers whose faults are worn away and whose doubts are cut, who are self-restrained and delight in the welfare of all beings, attain the stillness of Brahman.
source: Bhagavad Gita 5.25, Sanskrit Wikisource contributors, CC BY-SA, https://sa.wikisource.org/wiki/%E0%A4%AD%E0%A4%97%E0%A4%B5%E0%A4%A6%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%97%E0%A5%80%E0%A4%A4%E0%A4%BE/%E0%A4%95%E0%A4%B0%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%AE%E0%A4%B8%E0%A4%82%E0%A4%A8%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%AF%E0%A4%BE%E0%A4%B8%E0%A4%AF%E0%A5%8B%E0%A4%97%E0%A4%83; translation: Dharma Daily draft, pending review

words.meaning: whose doubts, whose dividedness, are cut
in the welfare of all beings

meaning: Notice the last qualification on the list: the sages who reach the highest stillness are the ones who delight in the good of every being. The verse quietly corrects a common picture of spirituality as a private escape — here, inner freedom and care for others arrive together, not in competition. The other marks are practical too: faults worn thin by practice, dividedness cut (no longer living two lives), the self reined in. For daily practice, the most actionable item is the last: do one thing today whose only beneficiary is someone else. Traditions differ over whether brahma-nirvana means merging into the one Self (Advaita) or a liberated soul's rest in the Lord (Vishishtadvaita, Dvaita); all agree it comes with, not despite, serving all beings.
reflection: Whose welfare, beyond your own circle, could your effort quietly serve today?

devanagari: भोक्तारं यज्ञतपसां सर्वलोकमहेश्वरम् । / सुहृदं सर्वभूतानां ज्ञात्वा मां शान्तिमृच्छति ॥5.29॥
iast: bhoktāraṃ yajñatapasāṃ sarvalokamaheśvaram । / suhṛdaṃ sarvabhūtānāṃ jñātvā māṃ śāntimṛcchati ॥5.29॥
sayIt: bhok-TAA-rum yug-nya-ta-pa-SAAM sar-va-LO-ka-ma-HAYSH-va-rum / su-HRI-dum sar-va-bhoo-TAA-naam GYAAT-vaa maam SHAAN-tim RICH-chha-ti
translation: Knowing Me as the enjoyer of all sacrifices and austerities, the great Lord of all the worlds, and the friend of every being, one reaches peace.
source: Bhagavad Gita 5.29, Sanskrit Wikisource contributors, CC BY-SA, https://sa.wikisource.org/wiki/%E0%A4%AD%E0%A4%97%E0%A4%B5%E0%A4%A6%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%97%E0%A5%80%E0%A4%A4%E0%A4%BE/%E0%A4%95%E0%A4%B0%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%AE%E0%A4%B8%E0%A4%82%E0%A4%A8%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%AF%E0%A4%BE%E0%A4%B8%E0%A4%AF%E0%A5%8B%E0%A4%97%E0%A4%83; translation: Dharma Daily draft, pending review

words.meaning: the great Lord of all the worlds

meaning: The closing verse of chapter five names three things to know about Krishna, and the order matters. The receiver of every offering: your efforts land somewhere, they are not shouted into a void. The Lord of all worlds: the outcomes were never yours to command anyway. And then the tenderest word — suhrid, a friend who wants your good without needing a reason. Peace, the verse says, follows from knowing that the one in charge is on your side. For daily practice, let one anxious effort today be handed to a friend rather than gripped. Devotional traditions (Vishishtadvaita, Dvaita) hear this as the Gita's heart — a personal Lord — while Advaita reads it as Ishvara, the saguna face of Brahman, meditated on for the same peace; the verse sustains both.
reflection: What burden becomes lighter if the results of your efforts already belong to a friend who wills your good?

devanagari: उद्धरेदात्मनात्मानं नात्मानमवसादयेत् । / आत्मैव ह्यात्मनो बन्धुरात्मैव रिपुरात्मनः ॥6.5॥
iast: uddharedātmanātmānaṃ nātmānamavasādayet । / ātmaiva hyātmano bandhurātmaiva ripurātmanaḥ ॥6.5॥
sayIt: ood-dha-ray-DAAT-ma-NAAT-maa-num NAAT-maa-na-ma-va-SAA-da-yet / aat-MY-va HYAAT-ma-no BUN-dhoo-raat-MY-va ri-poo-RAAT-ma-naha
translation: Let a person lift himself up by his own self; let him not drag himself down. For the self alone is the friend of the self, and the self alone is the enemy of the self.
source: Bhagavad Gita 6.5, Sanskrit Wikisource contributors, CC BY-SA, https://sa.wikisource.org/wiki/%E0%A4%AD%E0%A4%97%E0%A4%B5%E0%A4%A6%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%97%E0%A5%80%E0%A4%A4%E0%A4%BE/%E0%A4%86%E0%A4%A4%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%AE%E0%A4%B8%E0%A4%82%E0%A4%AF%E0%A4%AE%E0%A4%AF%E0%A5%8B%E0%A4%97%E0%A4%83; translation: Dharma Daily draft, pending review
meaning: The meditation chapter opens with responsibility: raise yourself by your own self, and do not drag yourself down. No teacher, ritual, or circumstance can do the inner work for you — and the verse names the reason. The same mind that talks you out of practice is the only instrument you have for practice; it is your closest friend and your nearest enemy, depending on how you train it. For daily life this closes two exits at once: waiting to be rescued, and blaming what happened to you. The one relationship you can never outsource is the one with your own mind, so tend it like the friendship it can become.
reflection: Where today did you talk yourself down when you could have lifted yourself up?

devanagari: बन्धुरात्मात्मनस्तस्य येनात्मैवात्मना जितः । / अनात्मनस्तु शत्रुत्वे वर्तेतात्मैव शत्रुवत् ॥6.6॥
iast: bandhurātmātmanastasya yenātmaivātmanā jitaḥ । / anātmanastu śatrutve vartetātmaiva śatruvat ॥6.6॥
sayIt: BUN-dhoo-RAAT-MAAT-ma-nus-TUS-ya yay-NAAT-my-VAAT-ma-naa ji-taha / a-NAAT-ma-nus-too SHUT-root-vay var-tay-TAAT-my-va SHUT-roo-vut
translation: For one who has conquered the self by the self, the self is a friend; but for one who has not mastered the self, the self itself acts in hostility, like an enemy.
source: Bhagavad Gita 6.6, Sanskrit Wikisource contributors, CC BY-SA, https://sa.wikisource.org/wiki/%E0%A4%AD%E0%A4%97%E0%A4%B5%E0%A4%A6%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%97%E0%A5%80%E0%A4%A4%E0%A4%BE/%E0%A4%86%E0%A4%A4%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%AE%E0%A4%B8%E0%A4%82%E0%A4%AF%E0%A4%AE%E0%A4%AF%E0%A5%8B%E0%A4%97%E0%A4%83; translation: Dharma Daily draft, pending review

words.meaning: but for one who has not mastered the self

meaning: This verse sharpens the point of the one before it by naming the deciding factor: mastery. For the person who has brought the mind under control by their own effort, that mind behaves like a trusted friend — it cooperates, steadies, encourages. For the person who has not, the very same mind works against them from the inside, exactly like an enemy. Nothing here is mystical; it is a plain diagnostic you can run today. Did your habits defend your intentions, or sabotage them? The verse refuses to blame fate for the answer: whether your mind is friend or enemy is settled by training, not by luck.
reflection: In which habit is your own mind currently acting more like an enemy than a friend?
